projects.name: aiseo-audit (agencyenterprise)
projects.language: TypeScript (Node >=20.19; deps cheerio, compromise, okapibm25, syllable, hedges, zod)
projects.last_activity: last commit 2026-10-22; v2.1.2; ~503 npm downloads in the month to 2026-10-18; 1 contributor (jpatterson933)
projects.what_to_adopt: The closest existing match to Module A. It runs fully locally and deterministically, with no LLM calls, and checks 50+ factors. Each factor sits in a FACTOR_REGISTRY entry with an evidence tier (supported / conditional / heuristic / diagnostic / experimental), citations to specific papers, a weight and a pipeline stage. The repo has docs/EVIDENCE.md plus a docs/paper-reviews/ folder with one review per paper (AutoGEO ICLR'26, C-SEO Bench NeurIPS'25, 'What Gets Cited' SIGIR'26, SAGEO Arena KDD'26, FeatGEO, Mind Reader, MAGEO, IF-GEO, and others). Users can edit weights per category in aiseo.config.json, and setting a weight to 0 excludes that category. Factors that map onto our checks: Numeric Claims, Citation Patterns, Quoted Attribution, Lead Summary, Direct Answer Statements, Heading Hierarchy, Answer Capsules (question-framed H2 followed by a short answer), Lists/Tables Presence, Section Length, and a Hedged Language penalty. Gates cap the score instead of adding points, and a 'polish gate' suppresses simplify-style advice on prose that is already fluent. This is the template for our 'evidence strength + source per check' column.
projects.caveats: The public API is URL-only (analyzeUrl/analyzeSitemap). Scoring a Markdown draft in the browser means lifting the factor functions out and swapping in a Markdown-to-HTML step. Cheerio and compromise both bundle for the browser, but that is untested. Their own evidence review downgrades lists, tables, question headings and answer capsules to unscored 'diagnostic' factors: they cite a causal null for formatting-only changes in 'What Gets Cited' (SIGIR 2026), and C-SEO Bench finding that mechanically added statistics lowered citation rank in 19 of 24 settings. That conflicts with the professor's check list, and we should check those paper claims ourselves before relying on them. The project has a single maintainer and only 8 stars, so it is young.

projects.name: answerlint
projects.last_activity: pushed 2026-10-21; v1.2.1; 55 npm downloads in the last month
projects.what_to_adopt: It takes a local Markdown or HTML file, a folder, a URL or a sitemap. 14 deterministic checks: direct answer in the first paragraph, Q&A density, readability, named entities, author byline, topical depth, trust signals, freshness, external citations, comparison content, citation likelihood, Wikidata entity density, and outbound-link health. Each finding reports evidence, a priority, the expected score impact and a recommended change. Weights live in .answerlintrc.json (custom_weights, aeo_weight/geo_weight), and users can add declarative rules such as required-term and forbidden-term. 'tui --watch ./article.md' re-runs the audit each time the file is saved, which is a working prototype of the Module C loop. The README states the principle in its own words: 'AnswerLint never rewrites your content silently... you keep editorial control.' 'audit --compare' reports against a competitor page, and diff/regression gates and SARIF output are included.
projects.caveats: Node-only (node-fetch, ora). Its check list is AEO/trust-oriented and has no explicit table, bullet-list or question-header checks. Very low adoption. Its 'citation likelihood' score is heuristic and not validated against outcomes.

projects.name: aeo-linter / @drowlink/aeo-linter-core
projects.language: TypeScript (core engine split from CLI; Chrome extension in extension/)
projects.what_to_adopt: A clean engine architecture copied from Lighthouse. Gatherers produce immutable typed artifacts (Headings, Chunks, JSON-LD, Links and so on), each audit is a pure function scoring 0 to 1, and an aggregator combines them. Our engine needs to run in both the browser and Node, and this layout separates the two well. Several audits map directly onto our checks: question-heading-alignment (headings phrased as user questions), table-list-scannability (table/ul/ol), fact-citation-density (percentages, metrics and citations), chunk-token-density (150 to 500 tokens), concise-answer-wordcount (30 to 60 words) and direct-definition-answering. Weights are listed per audit. The core ships as a separate npm package, and an unpacked Chrome extension is included.
projects.caveats: Only 2 months old with 4 stars and one author. Its thresholds (such as 30 to 60 words and 150 to 500 tokens) are asserted without sources. It works only on URLs and live DOM, with no Markdown draft input. The Chrome Web Store listing is still 'In Review'.

projects.name: geo-score (jianruntech)
projects.what_to_adopt: A published, versioned rubric (rubric/v1.1.md) with a separate evidence file that includes a section on where the evidence is thinnest. Its rule of 'two scores, never one' keeps the readiness score apart from the measured citation outcome, and Module A versus Module B should follow the same split. Content Citability is weighted 35 and covers self-contained answer passages, headings that match how people ask, sourced figures, bylines and freshness. The README reports a reproducibility test (the same list run three times in one day) and says to read a site's score as roughly ±5. Level 3 'watch' reports the cited rate with 95% Wilson intervals and paired-test diffs.
projects.caveats: Python, so any logic has to be re-implemented in TS. The star count fell from 619 to 32 between 2026-10-04 and today, which may mean a star purge, so do not use popularity as a signal. It is site-level (crawler access, schema, brand), not a draft analyzer. Live engines require the user's own API keys.

projects.name: GEO Optimizer (geo-optimizer-skill)
projects.what_to_adopt: A separate 0 to 100 Citability Score built from 47 content checks. 9 of them come straight from the methods tested in the KDD 2024 GEO paper; the list is in its docs/geo-methods, and every weight is in models/config.py. Its Content category covers H1, statistics, links, word count, heading hierarchy, lists/tables and front-loading. It also has a prompt-injection detector with 8 patterns (hidden text, invisible Unicode, LLM instructions in comments, micro-font and so on), which suits a 'trust' check, and a content-decay/evergreen predictor. 'geo fix' previews by default and writes only with --apply.
projects.caveats: Python, so we would port rules rather than depend on it. The repo is a funnel into the geoready.dev SaaS. Our 2026-10-04 teardown noted that it recommends '/llms.txt' even though no outcome evidence supports it, and that it misdescribes the OpenAI and Anthropic web-search APIs. Its scores mostly measure the site, not the draft.

projects.name: GEO (Princeton GEO-optim; KDD 2024 paper code + GEO-bench)
projects.what_to_adopt: The foundational paper (arXiv 2311.09735), whose methods underlie most of the professor's checks. src/geo_functions.py holds the GEO method prompts (Quotation Addition, Statistics Addition, Cite Sources, Fluency, Authoritative, Easy-to-understand, Technical Terms, Unique Words, plus a Keyword Stuffing baseline). These can become the suggestion types in the Module C side panel, presented as suggestions and never applied automatically. Its visibility metrics (position-adjusted word count, subjective impression) and the GEO-bench query plus source-page sets can serve as a fixed corpus for Module B's offline RAG simulator.
projects.caveats: The visibility gains in the paper are measured as word-count share, not citation odds. aiseo-audit's review also says that the '30 to 40% boost from quotes' figure comes from that word-count metric. The dataset is share-alike (CC-BY-SA), so a redistributed corpus needs the same license and attribution. The code is Python with old dependencies (Python 3.9).

projects.name: AutoGEO
projects.license: MIT (code); Researchy-GEO dataset MIT on HF (cx-cmu/Researchy-GEO)
projects.module: A (learned rules) + B (utility guardrail) + C (rule-based suggestions)
projects.what_to_adopt: ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2510.11438). It mines the content preferences of each engine (Gemini, GPT, Claude) from answer data in autogeo/rules/ (extractor, merger, explainer). The resulting rules, such as 'Conclusion First', can be shown as evidence-backed heuristics in Module A or as rule-cited suggestions in Module C. It scores both GEO (visibility) and GEU (utility), and that utility guardrail is a good metric to borrow for Module B. Datasets: E-commerce, GEO-Bench and Researchy-GEO, plus a Qwen 1.7B AutoGEO-Mini checkpoint.
projects.caveats: Its core output is an automatic rewrite of the whole document, which is the opposite of our 'never auto-rewrite' rule, so use only the rules and the metrics. Rules are specific to each engine and domain (its README says to re-extract them when the engine or dataset changes). Training AutoGEO-Mini needs 2 A100s.

projects.what_to_adopt: 'egeo fix-gaps' takes a tracker export (queries the page loses) and maps it to pages to fix, with a --dry-run preview. Its gap-report format is a useful reference for how Module B output could feed suggestions in Module C.

sweep.gaps:
1) No open tool scores an unpublished Markdown/HTML draft in the browser while showing an editable weight AND an evidence strength plus source for each check. aiseo-audit has the evidence registry but only accepts URLs and runs in Node. answerlint takes Markdown but runs in Node only and has no evidence tiers. We have to build a browser+Node engine (unified/remark parsing, pure check functions in the Lighthouse gatherer/audit style, a JSON evidence registry) ourselves.
2) No open GEO tool has a co-writing editor with side-by-side suggestions the author accepts or rejects. answerlint's TUI watch mode and Yoast's highlighting (GPL, reference only) are the nearest, and every LLM-based tool found (AutoGEO, eGEOagents, GEO-optim) rewrites the whole document. The suggestion model has to be ours: anchored to text ranges, citing the check and evidence it comes from, with accept/reject events logged and the source text never changed. That includes the optional Ollama wording layer.
3) Nobody has a 'frozen control group' offline RAG simulator, i.e. a free local model doing retrieval plus answers with citations over a fixed page set, with retrieval reported separately from citation. All the trackers call live engines with paid keys or scrape. The closest building blocks are the GEO-bench (CC-BY-SA) and AutoGEO Researchy-GEO (MIT) corpora and the GEO/GEU metrics.
4) Competitor feature extraction from the winning pages (word count, tables, schema), compared against the author's draft, exists only as answerlint's --compare between two URLs. A version that feeds the nightly job's results into the workspace needs to be built.
5) Evidence weakness to put in front of the professor: the evidence review in aiseo-audit, which cites 'What Gets Cited' (SIGIR 2026) and C-SEO Bench (NeurIPS 2025), finds no consistent causal effect for formatting-only changes (lists, tables, question headings) and finds that mechanically added statistics lowered citation rank in 19 of 24 settings. Several of the design's checks would therefore be honestly labelled 'diagnostic/weak'. We need to read those papers ourselves before relying on that.
sweep.notes: Method: I used the gh CLI (personal account) to pull repo metadata, READMEs and package.json files, npm download counts from api.npmjs.org, and HF dataset licenses. I opened every repo listed. WebSearch was used twice to find candidates. Status re-checks: elmohq/elmo was pushed 2026-10-23 and now has 486 stars; it is a brand tracker, out of scope for this angle, and its details are in the 2026-10-04 teardown. jianruntech/geo-score now shows 32 stars, against 619 in that teardown, so treat its popularity as unreliable. Not included: firecrawl/llmstxt-generator (540 stars, no LICENSE, dormant since 2025-06) and other llms.txt generators, because llms.txt has no outcome evidence (the aiseo-audit and Canonry docs agree); answerlint's 'llms generate/lint' covers it if we want it. GEORank (yaojingang, Apache-2.0, 510 stars) is a Chinese diagnosis-to-plan workbench with JSON-LD and llms.txt generators and a heavy stack (Postgres/Redis/Qdrant/Neo4j); it is reference only and I did not reopen it beyond metadata. Possible infrastructure (not GEO tools, metadata only): textlint (MIT, 3.2k stars), a pluggable rule engine for prose that runs in Node and the browser, could host Module A checks as rules. Recommended starting point: copy-adapt aiseo-audit's factor and evidence registry concept and DrowLink's gatherer/audit/aggregator split into a browser-safe TS core, take question-heading and table/list detection logic from DrowLink, and model Markdown input plus the 'never rewrite silently' UX on answerlint. All three are MIT, so keep their copyright notices in a THIRD_PARTY file. Scratch copies of the READMEs were kept in a temporary local folder, not committed.

projects.name: GEO (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024) reference code
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (code). Dataset is separate, see GEO-bench entry
projects.what_to_adopt: I read src/utils.py, src/generative_le.py, src/geo_functions.py and geval_prompts/. (1) For Module B, the original metric family: position-adjusted word count (impression_wordpos_count_simple). Each cited sentence scores its word count (words longer than 2 chars) times exp(-i/(N-1)) for sentence position, split across its co-citations, then normalized over the 5 sources. Alongside it are plain word count, position-only count and a paragraph-based variant. Also the citation regex \[[^\w\s]*\d+[^\w\s]*\] with nltk sentence splitting. Each of these is about 20 lines and easy to port to TS. (2) The answer-with-citations prompt (Perplexity-style: 'Every sentence ... immediately followed by an in-line citation ... [1][2][3]'). C-SEO Bench, AutoGEO and SAGEO Arena all reuse it, so it is the de-facto standard frozen-control prompt. (3) Seven G-Eval subjective-impression prompts on a 1-5 scale (influence, relevance, uniqueness, subjective position, subjective count, follow, diversity) for an optional LLM-judge metric. (4) The 9 GEO method prompts (authoritative, quotes, statistics, cite sources, fluency, unique words, technical terms, simple language, keyword stuffing). They map onto Module A checks as the evidence source for 'expert quotes', 'statistics density' and 'citations', and serve as suggestion templates for Module C.
projects.caveats: Apache-2.0 requires keeping the LICENSE/NOTICE attribution in ported files. The code calls the legacy openai<1.0 ChatCompletion API with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k at temperature 0.5, and it summarizes each source before answering. The PAWC exponential position decay is an assumption, not a measured quantity. Citations are 1-indexed (scores[cit-1]), whereas AutoGEO's port is 0-indexed, so pick one convention and test it. The evidence is fixed-context: the top 5 sources are already in the prompt, so these numbers say nothing about retrieval. Shares sum to 1, so one source's gain is another's loss.

projects.name: C-SEO Bench (Puerto et al., NeurIPS 2025 D&B)
projects.license: MIT (code); HF dataset parameterlab/c-seo-bench is Apache-2.0
projects.what_to_adopt: I read src/benchmark/engine.py, src/methods and notebook 3. Things to adopt: the Engine pattern (build prompt, batch, parse, store parquet) and get_citation_order(), a regex \[(\d+)\] that keeps dedup order and first-mention rank. The metric is citation-rank change of the boosted document against a no-method baseline, which is simpler and more robust than PAWC. The per-domain system prompts cover QA (web/news/debate) and product recommendation (retail/videogames/books) and add 'Search results are not sorted'. The adoption-rate protocol has several competitors using the same method. Six domain splits, roughly 16k queries with 10 docs each, Apache-2.0. Module A evidence: only 3 of 54 method-domain combinations were significantly positive, and moving a document's position in the context beat every rewrite. Module A should therefore show most content checks as weak evidence.
projects.caveats: The code depends on paid OpenAI/Anthropic batch APIs, which we would swap for Ollama. The README calls it 'experimental software'. The documents are third-party web/product text: check the dataset card provenance before redistributing it inside our repo, and prefer loading it from HF at runtime.

projects.name: SAGEO Arena (Kim et al., KDD 2026 per our corpus; arXiv 2602.12187)
projects.license: NO LICENSE file (all rights reserved); HF dataset yonsei-dli/SAGEO-Arena is MIT (queries + Google CSE result URLs only)
projects.what_to_adopt: This is the closest existing blueprint for the Module B frozen-control simulator: retrieve, rerank and generate over a fixed corpus, with visibility measured at every stage. Design ideas to reimplement (not copy): a multi-field BM25 with separate indices for title, meta_description, JSON-LD text, headings and body, fused by weighted RRF. Token chunks of 256 tokens with 64 overlap at sentence boundaries. A document's rank is its best chunk's rank. A neural reranker (Qwen3-Reranker-4B). A generator using the GEO prompt. Per-stage Hit@K, MRR, delta-rank and citation rate. Each experiment re-indexes only the edited target into the frozen corpus and diffs against a shared baseline. The crawler extracts the structural fields (httpx with a Playwright fallback). The dataset ships 9 domains x 300 queries (debate, ecommerce, fiqa, hotpotqa, msmarco, nfcorpus, nq, quora, researchy) and releases URLs rather than page text to avoid redistribution problems, a good pattern to copy as a policy. Module A evidence: body-only rewrites can hurt BM25 retrievability, structural fields help, and 'entity mirroring' into title and meta works. That argues for Module A metadata/heading checks.
projects.caveats: No license, so copy no code; reimplement from the paper and README description. Requires a GPU with vLLM (the reranker looks for 40 GB free), Java 21/Pyserini, and the paid OpenAI gpt-5-mini generator. 3 stars, so low maintenance. The MIT dataset includes queries from MS MARCO/NQ/HotpotQA and others, which carry their own upstream terms.

projects.name: AutoGEO (Wu, Zhong, Kim, Xiong, ICLR 2026)
projects.license: MIT (code); HF datasets cx-cmu/E-commerce, cx-cmu/GEO-Bench, cx-cmu/Researchy-GEO tagged MIT; AutoGEO_mini Qwen-1.7B checkpoints tagged MIT
projects.what_to_adopt: I read the README, autogeo/evaluation/generative_engine.py and metrics/geo_score.py. Adoptable pieces: (1) the rule-extraction pipeline (explainer, extractor, merger) that distills 'what this engine prefers' into a JSON rule list (root key filtered_rules). We could run it once against our own frozen local model to produce engine-specific evidence for Module A weights. (2) The GEO visibility score (a cleaned port of Aggarwal's PAWC) plus the GEU utility score, which checks that rewrites do not harm answer quality. Pair it with our visibility metric. (3) The Researchy-GEO and E-commerce query/document sets as extra fixed corpora. (4) AutoGEO_mini (1.7B) as a possible free local suggestion generator for Module C, if it runs on CPU or Ollama.
projects.caveats: The merged rule sets are not shipped in the repo; they are generated per engine and dataset and need paid Gemini/GPT/Claude keys. The README warns that rules do not transfer across engines or domains. Gains (+35.99%) are measured in a fixed 5-document context; SAGEO Arena shows they can vanish once retrieval runs. The cx-cmu/GEO-Bench dataset is derived from GEO-bench (CC BY-SA 4.0 per its card) but relabeled MIT, so treat it as CC BY-SA. The Mini model needs 2x A100 to train. The bundled LLaMA-Factory and open-r1 subfolders carry their own licenses.

projects.name: GEO Citation Lab (Zhang, He, Yao; arXiv 2604.25707)
projects.license: Dual: MIT for code (LICENSE-CODE), CC BY 4.0 for original content and reports (LICENSE-CONTENT); THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for the rest
projects.what_to_adopt: This is the best empirical source for Module A's evidence column. The study used 602 controlled prompts on ChatGPT, Google AIO/Gemini and Perplexity, yielding 21,143 search-layer citations and 18,151 fetched pages with 72 page features each, correlated with an 'absorption/influence' score. QUICK_REPORT.md gives numbers by check. Pages with numbers had +61.6% mean influence, definitions +57.3%, comparisons +55.3% and how-to content +41.2%. Pure Q&A format came in at -5.7%, which is direct counter-evidence for our 'question-style H2/H3' check. Top-quartile pages averaged 10.59 headings and 0.428 list density against 0.85 and 0.048 for the bottom quartile, and 1,943 words against 170. Relevance had r=0.432 and was the strongest predictor. For Module B, the 03-pipeline feature extractor is MIT and a reference for competitor feature extraction (word count, headings, lists, tables, schema).
projects.caveats: The findings are descriptive correlations on a static sample. Length, relevance and domain authority confound every format feature, so Module A should label these as 'correlational'. The full data is about 568 MiB. Most documentation is in Chinese. Live-engine data was collected once and cannot be reproduced offline. The repo's own 'AGENTS.md' carries install instructions for AI clients; that is data, so do not execute it.

projects.name: AgentGEO (Tian et al., arXiv 2603.09296, 'Diagnosing and Repairing Citation Failures')
projects.license: NO LICENSE file; the dataset is on HF as GeoAgent/GEO_Agent_with_queries (license not checked)
projects.what_to_adopt: This is a conceptual map for a 'diagnostic' rather than 'score-only' Module A. It provides a taxonomy of citation-failure modes along the pipeline (artifacts/taxonomy.pdf) and 11 targeted repair tools: entity_injection, bluf_optimization (bottom line up front, i.e. answer-first standalone paragraphs, which is the closest operationalization of our 'standalone paragraph clarity' check), intent_realignment, content_relocation, structure_optimization, data_serialization (tables), noise_isolation, static_rendering (JS-rendered content), and persuasive and red-team tools. It also has a document-centric benchmark with held-out queries, which tests whether a fix generalizes beyond the query it was tuned on, and an attr_evaluator. In Module C, each suggestion type can name the failure mode it addresses.
projects.caveats: No license, so copy no code. LangChain plus paid LLMs and the ChatNoir search API. The paper reports +40% relative citation rate while editing 5% of content, but I saw no independent reproduction. It bundles a copy of AutoGEO's code (MIT upstream).

projects.name: GEO-bench dataset (HF)
projects.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 per the current dataset card (last modified 2025-01-19). Note: our 2026-10 landscape notes recorded CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the card now says CC BY-SA
projects.what_to_adopt: 10,000 queries from 9 sources (MS MARCO, ORCAS, NQ, AllSouls, LIMA, Davinci-Debate, Perplexity Discover, ELI5, GPT-4 generated), tagged by domain, difficulty and intent, each with 5 cleaned top-Google result texts. Use the queries and tags as an evaluation query pool for the frozen control, and the 5-source groups as a fixed-context smoke test for reproducing PAWC.

The source texts are third-party web pages under their owners' copyright, and the upstream query sets have their own terms (MS MARCO's are non-commercial research). projects.name: E-GEO (Bagga et al., arXiv 2511.20867)
projects.license: Code: NO LICENSE file. Data: HF psbagga17/E-GEO tagged CC BY 4.0 (products come from Amazon Reviews 2023, which has its own terms)
projects.what_to_adopt: Ideas only. The rewriter is query-blind and fact-preserving and is scored by rank delta (original minus rewritten rank among 10 candidates) under 5 judge LLMs, a clean, simple metric. The '15 best optimized rewriting prompts' in src/optimized_prompts.json could inspire suggestion phrasing. There is also a feature-presence heatmap (initial vs optimized), and a 14-attack adversarial benchmark with judge flag rates, useful for teaching Module C what not to suggest (manipulative edits). There is a public leaderboard with a PR submission flow.
projects.caveats: No code license. Product-recommendation domain only. All judges are paid APIs (GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama 4). Do not confuse it with the unrelated PyPI package 'egeo'.

projects.name: ALCE (Gao et al., EMNLP 2023) citation evaluation
projects.what_to_adopt: Citation recall and precision via NLI (compute_autoais in eval.py). A sentence's citations count as 'supporting' if the cited passages entail it. That turns Module B's 'was the creator's page cited' into 'was it cited and actually supporting'. It flags the hallucinated or spurious citations that GEO's PAWC silently counts.
projects.caveats: It uses google/t5_xxl_true_nli_mixture (11B), too heavy for a free nightly GitHub Actions job. Substitute a small NLI cross-encoder or an Ollama judge and validate the agreement. The codebase is dormant since 2024. It is Python, so we would port the metric logic only.

projects.name: MAGEO (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2604.19516)
projects.what_to_adopt: Protocol ideas. The Twin Branch Evaluation runs the original and the edited document under identical conditions, which attributes visibility change causally to the edit. That is exactly how Module B should report 'did this accepted suggestion help', using paired runs with shared seeds. Also: the DSV-CF metric family, which combines semantic visibility with citation fidelity and attribution accuracy, and a 'fidelity gate' that rejects candidate edits that break faithfulness. The latter is a good safeguard for Module C suggestions.
projects.caveats: No license. LiteLLM plus paid engines. 'Core method only' research code. I did not check where the MSME-GEO-Bench data is released.

projects.license: Repo: NO LICENSE file. Dataset huggingface.co/datasets/lmarena-ai/search-arena-24k: user prompts CC-BY-4.0; model outputs governed by provider terms

The CC-BY-4.0 user prompts are a realistic, license-clean source of queries for the frozen control's query set. The paper's findings that users prefer more citations and that models often mis-attribute citations support Module B's citation-fidelity check.

projects.name: Ragnarok (castorini, TREC RAG baseline framework)
projects.what_to_adopt: A reference RAG pipeline (retrieve, rerank, generate attributed answers) from the TREC RAG track, with cited-segment output formats. It is a license-clean reference for the shape of Module B's answer record (answer sentences, each with cited doc ids) and for TREC-style run files, if we ever want our nightly results comparable with IR tooling.
projects.caveats: Python with Pyserini/Java; version 0.0.1. It targets the MS MARCO v2.1 segment corpus, not a creator's page set. Use it for format and design, not as a dependency of a TS project.

projects.name: ConflictingQA / 'What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing?' (Wan et al., ACL 2024)
projects.license: MIT (code); data is a pickled DataFrame on Google Drive containing scraped page text (third-party copyright)
projects.what_to_adopt: Counter-evidence for Module A weights. The paper found that LLMs resolving conflicting sources lean on query relevance and largely ignore stylistic credibility cues such as scientific references and a neutral tone. Cite it in the evidence panel for the 'citations/sources' and 'expert quotes' checks so their default weights stay modest. Its 512-token 'most relevant window' selection mirrors chunk-level retrieval.

projects.what_to_adopt: The best fit for Module C. It is a Markdown-native WYSIWYG editor built on ProseMirror and remark, so drafts round-trip as Markdown and Module A's mdast positions line up with the editor. plugin-diff has the exact accept/reject API we need: startDiffReviewCmd(modifiedMarkdown) parses a proposed Markdown version and displays it as a pending diff over the author's doc. It also exports acceptDiffChunkCmd, rejectDiffChunkCmd, acceptDiffRangeCmd, rejectDiffRangeCmd, acceptAllDiffsCmd, clearDiffReviewCmd, getPendingChanges and computeDocDiff. Crepe's AI feature takes a pluggable AIProvider = (context, signal) => AsyncIterable<string> of Markdown tokens, so an Ollama stream drops straight in. The accept/reject labels are configurable.

For our 'never auto-rewrite' rule, skip the streaming path: build the suggested Markdown off-document and call startDiffReviewCmd yourself. sweep.gaps:
No open-source project gives us Module C's core product: GEO-specific suggestions that each carry evidence. All the editors above supply the mechanics (diff, suggestion marks, accept/reject commands) but not the content of a suggestion, its link to a check, or its evidence. We must build:
(1) A suggestion model: each card links to a Module A check id, the exact source range (mdast position), a before/after Markdown snippet, the score change if accepted, an evidence-strength badge with its citation, and a status (pending/accepted/rejected/dismissed-forever), plus persistence that survives re-analysis. Positions shift after every author edit, so anchors must be re-mapped (ProseMirror mapping, or re-matching after re-parse).
(2) Templated suggestion generators per check: question-style header rewrites, convert-to-list, a table scaffold from inline numbers, citation and quote placeholders, standalone-paragraph rewrites. They run deterministically without an LLM. Optional Ollama wording goes through a provider adapter that only ever returns proposed Markdown and never touches the doc.
(3) A firm 'no auto-write' rule enforced in code: the doc changes only through an explicit accept action. This means disabling the 'insert/stream into doc' defaults in Milkdown Crepe AI and Plate AI. Add a test that asserts the document is byte-identical until accept.
(4) A side-by-side layout: suggestion rail and diff cards (react-diff-viewer-continued / jsdiff, or Milkdown plugin-diff inline), a live score panel with editable weights, and keyboard accept/reject with focus states.
(5) A merged diagnostics pipeline that turns Module A check results, Harper lints and optional retext messages into one positioned message list for the editor (the vfile message shape is the natural common format).
(6) An accept/reject telemetry log kept locally or exported: this is the human-AI interaction data the design doc's research angle needs. No editor ships this.
sweep.notes:
Method: I read the prior teardown (the project's earlier landscape notes, 2026-10-04, not published) and found no editor coverage there, so none of this repeats it. Repo metadata came from the gh REST API, versions and licenses from the npm registry (2026-10-23). I read source and docs directly: Milkdown plugin-diff and Crepe AI source, the Plate suggestion and AI docs in the repo, the prosemirror-suggest-changes README, the @codemirror/merge type definitions, the harper.js package type definitions and docs, the Tiptap pricing and AI Suggestion pages, and the CKEditor and Yoast license files.

Recommended stack for one week:
- Milkdown (MIT, Markdown-native, remark-based like Module A) with @milkdown/plugin-diff's startDiffReviewCmd(suggestedMarkdown) for inline accept/reject.
- A suggestion rail using jsdiff and react-diff-viewer-continued.
- harper.js in a Web Worker for grammar hints.
- @codemirror/merge as an optional 'source mode'.
Fallback if Milkdown's diff proves brittle: Tiptap MIT core with @handlewithcare/prosemirror-suggest-changes. That is the same pattern BlockNote's GPL AI package uses, rebuilt from MIT parts. Plate is the strongest batteries-included React option, but it is Slate-based, so choose it instead of the ProseMirror stack, not alongside it.

License flags:
- Paid: Tiptap Pro (Tracked Changes and the AI Toolkit are custom-priced; no free plan), Plate Plus, CKEditor premium.
- GPL, reference only: Yoast yoastseo, BlockNote xl-*, CKEditor core.
- LGPL: LanguageTool.
- MPL-2.0 (usable with care): BlockNote core.

Ecosystem change: ProseMirror and CodeMirror GitHub repos were archived in April 2026 and moved to code.haverbeke.berlin. The npm packages are still published normally (prosemirror-view 1.42.7 on 2026-10-22).

Not verified: platejs.org docs pages returned HTTP 500, so the Plate claims rest on the repo's own .mdx docs and source. I did not run any of these in a Next.js build, so Harper's 19 MB WASM against Vercel static limits and Milkdown inside React/Next both need a quick spike on day 1.

projects.name: @ijonis/geo-lint
projects.what_to_adopt: This is the closest existing TypeScript GEO rule set: 97 rules, 36 of them GEO, run over .md/.mdx files. Port its rule functions and starting thresholds from src/utils/geo-analyzer.ts and src/rules/geo-*.ts into our AST-based checks: countQuestionHeadings (wh-word list; 20% of H2/H3 should be questions), analyzeLeadSentences / weak-lead starts (direct answer after a heading), countStatistics (regexes for %, multipliers, currency, 4+ digit numbers, million/billion; 1 stat per 500 words expected), hasMarkdownTable (applies above 1,000 words), analyzeCitationBlocks (40+ word first paragraph per H2), countSourceCitations (citation phrases), hasExpertQuote (blockquote plus an em-dash attribution), and hasFAQSection. Each violation carries a fixStrategy/suggestion string, a good model for Module C suggestion text. Runtime deps are only gray-matter and jiti, and the rule functions are pure string-in, number-out, so they run in the browser.
projects.last_activity: last commit 2026-03-19 (v0.2.1 on npm); quiet for about 7 months
projects.caveats: Checks are regexes over raw markdown strings, not an AST, so they are brittle (for example, /\d{4,}/ counts years as statistics). Thresholds are author heuristics with no cited evidence, so we must attach our own evidence strength and source per check. The README says its readability and transition-word analysis is 'inspired by Yoast SEO' (GPL-3.0). Do not copy src/data/transition-words-*.ts or the readability helpers; copy only the GEO analyzers, with MIT attribution. The npm bundle is 112.6 KB gz because it includes the CLI, so vendor the functions instead of depending on the package. Small project, effectively one maintainer.

projects.name: compromise (compromise/three)
projects.what_to_adopt: Rule-based English NLP that runs in the browser. The parts we need: .numbers() and percentages (written-out numbers like 'five million', units, ordinal vs cardinal) to make statistics density more precise than geo-lint's regexes; .quotations() (src/3-three/misc/quotations) and .parentheses() for explicit quote detection; sentences().isQuestion() (src/3-three/sentences/questions.js) for question-style headers that do not end in '?'; .people() / .organizations() to detect the attribution in an expert quote ('said Dr. Jane Smith, CTO of X'); and .pronouns() to flag paragraphs that open with an unresolved 'this/it/they', a cheap standalone-clarity signal. Tiered builds: compromise/one is the tokenizer only, /two adds POS tagging, /three adds the accessor APIs.
projects.caveats: Full build is 147.5 KB gz (357 KB minified), so lazy-load it after the first paint. English only. The tagger is heuristic, so numbers inside table cells or code should be excluded by running it only on paragraph text taken from the AST.

projects.name: wink-nlp + wink-eng-lite-web-model
projects.what_to_adopt: Alternative or complement to compromise when we need typed entities. Its entities() API returns date, ordinal, cardinal, money, percent, time, duration, email and url, a clean basis for a 'numeric statistics per 100 words' measure with typed evidence. It also gives sentence boundary detection, a built-in Flesch reading ease score, a BM25 vectorizer and cosine similarity. The BM25 vectorizer can be reused as the offline lexical retriever in Module B's frozen RAG simulator, so the same engine runs in Node and the browser. TypeScript types are included.
projects.caveats: The library is only 11.5 KB gz, but the English model wink-eng-lite-web-model is about 1.01 MB gz (3.8 MB minified). It is too heavy for the editor's first load, so in the browser use it in a Web Worker or only in Node/Module B. Pick one of compromise or wink as the primary browser NLP to avoid shipping both.

projects.name: words/* readability formulas (flesch, automated-readability, dale-chall-formula, coleman-liau, gunning-fog, syllable) and retext-readability
projects.what_to_adopt: Tiny, pure formula functions that take counts and return a score: flesch is 0.23 KB gz, automated-readability 0.24 KB, dale-chall-formula 0.39 KB, and syllable is 6.1 KB gz for syllable counts. They supply a readability sub-score per paragraph, which feeds standalone paragraph clarity. If we want readability warnings anchored to sentences, retext-readability (https://github.com/retextjs/retext-readability, MIT, 18.6 KB gz) is a unified plugin that applies Dale-Chall, ARI, Coleman-Liau, Flesch, Gunning-Fog, SMOG and Spache against a target age (default 16) and emits positioned vfile messages. Those messages plug straight into the same unified pipeline and into Module C's evidence highlighting.
projects.last_activity: words/* last pushed Nov 2022; retext-readability Sep 2023 (stable, feature-complete)
projects.caveats: The words/* repos are dormant but tiny and deterministic, so low risk. Readability formulas are not evidence-backed GEO signals, so give them a low default weight and say so in the check's evidence-strength field. English only.

projects.name: sentence-splitter (textlint)
projects.what_to_adopt: Splits English and Japanese text into sentences, returns an AST with positions, and attaches 'contexts' to quote pairs (it deliberately keeps 'He said "This is a pen. I like it"' as one sentence). Use it to split paragraph text into sentences for per-sentence statistics and readability, and its quote-pair contexts as a second signal for explicit quote detection. 4.7 KB gz.
projects.caveats: Quoted multi-sentence spans stay merged by design. The zero-byte fallback is the platform's Intl.Segmenter with sentence granularity, built into evergreen browsers and modern Node; I did not open a page for it, so this comes from general knowledge.

projects.name: Transformers.js (@huggingface/transformers) + Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (library); the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 weights are Apache-2.0 per the upstream sentence-transformers card (not re-verified this pass)
projects.what_to_adopt: In-browser and Node sentence embeddings through the feature-extraction pipeline. Two ways to score standalone paragraph self-containedness: (1) embed each paragraph alone and with its preceding context, then measure the similarity drop; or (2) treat the paragraph's own H2/H3 question as a query and check that the paragraph alone retrieves it. That mirrors what an AI engine does when it lifts one chunk. The same model and code give Module B's offline RAG simulator its dense retriever, so the Module A score and the Module B outcome share one embedding space. The library is 165 KB gz and the quantized ONNX model (model_quantized.onnx / model_int8.onnx) is 23 MB, downloaded once and cached by the browser.
projects.caveats: Must be optional and lazy-loaded, ideally in a Web Worker, because a 23 MB download cannot sit on the critical path. The rule-based checks need to work without it. WebGPU is optional and it falls back to WASM. Embedding-similarity heuristics for self-containedness are our own invention, so mark the evidence strength as 'exploratory'.

projects.name: htmlmetaparser (+ htmlparser2)
projects.what_to_adopt: A streaming htmlparser2 handler that extracts JSON-LD, microdata, RDFa, OpenGraph, Twitter cards, oEmbed and HTML meta in one pass. That covers the 'schema present?' check for HTML drafts and Module B's competitor 'schema' feature (FAQPage, HowTo, Article, Organization) with one code path. Its 15.1 KB gz plus htmlparser2's 34.7 KB gz is far lighter than structured-data-testing-tool (105 KB gz, last pushed 2023) or web-auto-extractor (80.7 KB gz, last pushed 2022).
projects.caveats: Small, single-maintainer project. Pinned to htmlparser2 ^9 while 12.0.0 is current, so expect a duplicate htmlparser2 in the bundle unless we dedupe. GitHub shows the license as NOASSERTION, but package.json says Apache-2.0. Markdown drafts have no schema, so for them the check becomes a suggestion to add JSON-LD.

projects.name: schema-dts
projects.what_to_adopt: TypeScript type definitions for the whole schema.org vocabulary, 0.2 KB at runtime. Use them to type-check the extracted JSON-LD (FAQPage, QAPage, HowTo, Article with author and citation) and to generate correctly typed JSON-LD snippets that Module C offers as an accept/reject suggestion, for example 'add FAQPage markup built from your question headers'.
projects.caveats: Types only, with no runtime validation, so a malformed live JSON-LD block still needs our own guards. Use as a dev dependency.

projects.name: @mozilla/readability
projects.what_to_adopt: Firefox Reader View's main-content extraction. When the input is a full HTML page (a pasted URL or saved page, and every competitor page in Module B), run it first to strip nav, footer and boilerplate so the GEO checks score the article, not the chrome. 11.2 KB gz and no dependencies.
projects.caveats: Needs a DOM: the native one in the browser, linkedom (ISC, 75.4 KB gz, https://github.com/WebReflection/linkedom) or jsdom (MIT, much heavier) in Node. Its output is cleaned HTML, which then goes through rehype-parse and rehype-remark into mdast. Skip it for Markdown drafts.

projects.name: jsonld.js
projects.what_to_adopt: Optional JSON-LD expansion and flattening, so @graph arrays, nested @context and compacted IRIs normalize to plain schema.org types before we count FAQPage, author and citation properties. Without it, a schema check that only reads the top-level @type misses @graph-wrapped markup, which Yoast and Rank Math emit.
projects.caveats: 30.2 KB gz. Remote @context loading must be disabled (use a static schema.org context) so it does not make network calls and stays deterministic. Fine to defer to v1.1. In v1 a JSON.parse plus a walk over @graph covers most pages.

projects.name: yoastseo (in Yoast/wordpress-seo monorepo)
projects.what_to_adopt: Design reference only: how a mature content-analysis library structures 'researches' (metrics) separately from 'assessments' (scored, colored checks with feedback text), and how it handles sentence length, paragraph length, subheading distribution and transition-word assessments. That separation is a good model for our check registry: metric, then evidence, then weighted score.
projects.caveats: GPL-3.0 copyleft: do not copy code or word lists. Doing so would force our MIT project under GPL. Also 133.5 KB gz and built around WordPress and SEO keyphrases, not GEO.

projects.name: jianruntech/geo-score
projects.what_to_adopt: Status recheck: still active (pushed 2026-10-23, 32 stars, site geo-score.dev). It is Python with zero dependencies, providing a CLI, a GitHub Action and an MCP server, plus a 0-100 readiness rubric and citation tracking on the user's own API keys. Use it as the comparison baseline for our GEO Score's rubric and its Wilson-interval reporting, and as the outside 'open rubric' to benchmark against in the write-up. Its logic is not usable as a TS dependency.
projects.caveats: Not TypeScript. It overlaps our positioning (a free GEO score), so our edge has to come from per-check evidence strength, editable weights and the human-in-the-loop workspace, not the score itself. Small new project (created 2026-09-08).

projects.name: cheerio
projects.what_to_adopt: Keep it for Module B's Node-side competitor page feature extraction (word count, tables, schema script tags) only if a jQuery-style API is easier there than hast. For Module A, the unified/hast pipeline already does this, and cheerio would add a second HTML model to the browser bundle.
projects.caveats: 118.9 KB gz, and it duplicates parse5/htmlparser2, which we already ship. Prefer one AST (mdast/hast) across Modules A, B and C so that features and evidence positions line up.

sweep.gaps:
No open-source JS/TS project implements these, so we have to build them:
(1) An evidence-annotated check registry. Each GEO check needs a stated evidence strength and source (for example the GEO paper, Aggarwal et al., arXiv 2311.09735, for statistics, quotations and citations), a default weight and a user-editable weight. geo-lint and Yoast hard-code thresholds with no evidence attached, and geo-score's rubric is Python.
(2) A standalone paragraph clarity score. Nothing off the shelf scores whether a chunk survives being lifted out of the page. We must combine: unresolved anaphora at the paragraph start (compromise pronouns/determiners such as 'this', 'it', 'these', 'the above'), a length window, a readability sub-score, whether the paragraph restates the subject of its heading, and an optional embedding test (paragraph alone versus with context, using transformers.js).
(3) Expert quote detection: a quote span (blockquote node, quotation marks via compromise or sentence-splitter), plus an attribution (person or organization entity and a speech verb within N tokens), plus a credential cue. geo-lint only matches a blockquote followed by an em dash.
(4) Citation/source classification: separating inline links, footnotes, 'according to X (year)' phrases and bare URLs, and judging whether a link is a primary source (.gov, .edu, doi.org, arxiv) or self-promotion.
(5) Statistic detection that is aware of the AST (skip code, tables and dates) and typed (percent, money, cardinal with unit), and that de-duplicates regex hits against NER hits.
(6) The scoring engine and weight UI: normalization per check, length gating as in geo-lint (500, 800 and 1,000-word floors), aggregation into the GEO Score, and an explanation trace.
(7) A mapping from mdast positions to the editor's ranges, so Module C can show evidence highlights and side-by-side accept/reject suggestions without ever rewriting the author's text.
(8) Calibration: linking Module A sub-scores to Module B's retrieved-or-cited outcomes from the frozen local RAG simulator, so weights can later be fit, or at least checked, against our own data.
sweep.notes:
All license, star and push data come from the GitHub API on 2026-10-23. Bundle sizes are gzipped figures from the Bundlephobia API for each package's latest version. The prior teardown (the project's earlier landscape notes, 2026-10-04, not published) covered Elmo and product positioning, not TS parsing or NLP libraries, so nothing here repeats it. Elmo's own README admits it has 'no on-page content audits', which confirms that Module A fills a gap.

Recommended browser budget for Module A's core: unified, remark-parse and remark-gfm (about 30 KB), rehype-dom-parse and rehype-remark (about 17 KB), sentence-splitter (5 KB), the words/* formulas and syllable (about 7 KB), htmlmetaparser and htmlparser2 (about 50 KB), and compromise lazy-loaded (148 KB). That totals roughly 110 KB gz before compromise and about 260 KB with it. Transformers.js (165 KB plus a 23 MB model) stays opt-in in a Web Worker.

Choose between compromise and wink-nlp. Recommendation: compromise in the browser (quotations, questions, numbers, people); wink-nlp in Node or Module B, where its 1 MB model does not matter and its BM25 vectorizer can serve as the frozen offline retriever.

Rejected after opening: structured-data-testing-tool (ISC, 105 KB gz, last pushed 2023-07), web-auto-extractor (MIT, 80.7 KB gz, last pushed 2022-06), readability-scores (MIT, last release 2020-05), text-readability (ISC, no repo listed on npm), and madeburo/GEO-AI (MIT, 11 stars, focused on llms.txt and crawler rules rather than content scoring).

License flag: geo-lint is MIT but credits Yoast (GPL-3.0) for its readability and transition-word analysis. Copy only its GEO analyzers, never its data/transition-words files.

projects.name: kepano/defuddle (+ linkedom as the Node DOM)
projects.module: B (competitor feature extraction), A (HTML input normalization)
projects.what_to_adopt: The main-content extractor for fetched pages. `defuddle/node` accepts any DOM Document (linkedom, JSDOM or happy-dom) and returns cleaned HTML or Markdown, plus `wordCount`, `schemaOrgData` (raw schema.org JSON-LD) and other metadata. That covers the 'word count, schema' competitor features directly. Count tables, lists, headings and stats from the cleaned HTML with the same checks as Module A, so A and B share one feature extractor. The CLI (`npx defuddle parse --markdown --json`) is handy for fixtures. The README says it can replace Mozilla Readability.
projects.caveats: Pre-1.0 (0.19.x), so pin the version. Needs `"type": "module"`. I did not check whether its cleanup strips any tables or quote blocks, so test against the Module A checks. A fallback is https://github.com/mozilla/readability (Apache-2.0, 11.5k stars, npm 0.6.0 dated 2025-03, slower release cadence). Neither runs JS-rendered pages, so plain fetch only (no Playwright) in v1.

projects.name: MiniSearch
projects.what_to_adopt: A tiny, dependency-free BM25-style full-text index that runs the same in Node and the browser. Use it as the 'retrieval' half of the offline RAG simulator: index the fixed page set (chunked by paragraph or section) and take the top-k chunks per query into the citation prompt. It is deterministic, so a frozen control group stays frozen.
projects.caveats: Lexical only. For hybrid retrieval, add embeddings from transformers.js (below) and fuse the scores yourself (RRF), or use Orama. lunr (https://github.com/olivernn/lunr.js, MIT, last npm 2023) and wink-bm25-text-search (https://github.com/winkjs/wink-bm25-text-search, MIT, last activity 2022-11) are both staler, so avoid them.

projects.name: Orama
projects.license: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.md; GitHub shows NOASSERTION only because the file is .md)
projects.what_to_adopt: Choose it over MiniSearch if you want BM25 plus vector plus hybrid search in one in-memory engine (`mode: 'fulltext'|'vector'|'hybrid'`, `vector[N]` schema fields). It also has plugin-data-persistence to snapshot the index into the repo, so the control group's index is literally frozen and diffable. Works in Node and the browser.
projects.caveats: The company's focus has moved toward its cloud product, so stick to the OSS core package. The @orama/plugin-embeddings plugin brings its own model stack; generating vectors with transformers.js and passing them in is simpler and more controllable. Pick only one of MiniSearch and Orama.

projects.name: huggingface/transformers.js
projects.module: B (embeddings for dense or hybrid retrieval), C (optional in-browser)
projects.what_to_adopt: The `feature-extraction` pipeline gives local sentence embeddings over ONNX in Node (CPU) and the browser (WASM or WebGPU), with `dtype` q8 or q4 quantization. Use a small permissively licensed embedding model (for example an all-MiniLM or bge-small ONNX port) for the dense half of the simulator's retriever. No API key, and it runs fine on a CPU runner. Cache the HF model dir in actions/cache.
projects.caveats: Models download from the HF hub on first use, so pin the revision. Check each embedding model's license separately (for example EmbeddingGemma uses Gemma terms, not OSI). By default the browser loads WASM binaries from a CDN; self-host them for the Vercel static site. Ollama `embed()` is an alternative that avoids a second runtime.

projects.name: node-llama-cpp
projects.what_to_adopt: An in-process GGUF runtime with no daemon. It ships prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows and falls back to cmake builds without node-gyp. It can force output to a JSON schema through grammar-constrained decoding, and also does function calling, embeddings and reranking. A schema such as {answer_sentences:[{text, cites:[int]}]} removes regex-parsing failures, which matters with 1-4B models. Use it if Ollama's service setup in Actions is flaky, or if you want exact token-level control.
projects.caveats: Node only (not the browser). You manage GGUF downloads yourself (pin the HF URL and sha256). Pick one runtime as the primary to keep the control group frozen. I'd make Ollama the default for contributor ergonomics and offer this as an adapter.

projects.name: samclarke/robots-parser + ai-robots-txt/ai.robots.txt (bot registry)
projects.module: B (fetch eligibility + competitor audit), A (eligibility check)
projects.what_to_adopt: robots-parser says it aims to comply with RFC 9309: wildcards and `$`, isAllowed / isDisallowed / isExplicitlyDisallowed, getMatchingLineNumber (shows the user the exact rule line), getCrawlDelay, getSitemaps. Use it to (a) make our own fetcher polite and (b) report a per-AI-bot allow/deny verdict for the creator's and the competitors' pages. ai.robots.txt/robots.json lists 195 agents with operator, respect, function and description, including OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User-style user agents, Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User. Vendor a pinned snapshot as the bot list, split into search / user-fetch / training roles.
projects.last_activity: robots-parser npm 3.0.1 from 2023, repo maintained (commit 2026-10-08); registry pushed 2026-10-23
projects.caveats: Many registry fields say 'Unclear at this time', so don't present them as fact. The registry is built to block bots, so it doesn't verify claims about which bots respect robots.txt. Google's C++ reference parser (https://github.com/google/robotstxt, Apache-2.0) is useful only as a conformance test oracle.

projects.name: AKzar1el/mcp-geo (DigestSEO) SQLite schema
projects.what_to_adopt: The closest TS/SQLite citation-tracker schema I found. migrations/0001_initial.sql has brands, prompts (intent_stage, shape), runs (engine, mode, status, prompts_total/completed, cost estimate, error), prompt_responses (raw_response, brand_mentioned, brand_cited_with_link, cited_urls_json, competitors_mentioned_json) and a shared_prompt_cache keyed on (prompt_hash, engine, model). 0003 adds engine_citations_json, keeping engine-native citations apart from URLs extracted from the text. Copy the run/response split and the native-vs-extracted citation columns. Our 'engine' is 'local-sim:<model@digest>'.
projects.caveats: Small one-maintainer project tied to a paid EUR 99 audit upsell. It has a users/stripe table we don't need. No retrieval-rank or 'consulted vs cited' column, no seed or temperature column, no corpus or index version, so add those for the frozen-control design.

projects.name: elmohq/elmo (re-checked: schema pattern only)
projects.what_to_adopt: Status: active (pushed 2026-10-23, 486 stars). Borrow one pattern from packages/lib/src/db/schema.ts: `prompt_runs` keeps the immutable rawOutput, model and webQueries, while `run_extractions`, `run_mentions` and `citations` (url, domain, model, pageId -> normalized `cited_pages`) are derived tables that 'can be thrown away and re-derived' when the extractor changes. Apply the same split to our JSONL plus SQLite store, with raw sim outputs append-only and metrics recomputed from them.
projects.caveats: Built for agency brand tracking with scraped consumer UIs (already covered in our 2026-10-04 teardown). Postgres-centric and much heavier than we need. Copying the MIT code is allowed, but we only need the idea.

projects.name: better-sqlite3 (or built-in node:sqlite) + JSONL in repo
projects.what_to_adopt: Recommended storage: the nightly job appends raw runs as JSONL committed to the repo (diffable, works with no server, and the Vercel site can read it at build time), then rebuilds a SQLite file from the JSONL for queries. better-sqlite3 (v13.0.3, 2026-08) is synchronous, fast and has prebuilt binaries. The zero-dependency option is Node's built-in `node:sqlite`: unflagged since v22.13 / v23.4, and 'Stability 1.2 Release candidate' since v25.7.0 according to the Node docs. For vectors, sqlite-vec (npm 0.1.9, MIT/Apache) is optional. For analytics, @duckdb/node-api (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-node-neo, MIT, 2.0.0-r.1 from 2026-10-21) can query the JSONL directly.
projects.caveats: node:sqlite is still not 'stable', so on Node 24 LTS expect experimental warnings. Pick better-sqlite3 unless avoiding native deps matters more. Don't commit the .db file; regenerate it. DuckDB's node-api is a young rewrite, so make it optional.

projects.name: mlc-ai/web-llm and ngxson/wllama (in-browser LLM for Module C)
projects.module: C (optional suggestion wording in the browser), not B
projects.what_to_adopt: If Module C should reword suggestions with no Ollama install and no server, WebLLM (WebGPU, v0.2.86 on 2026-10-11, OpenAI-style API) or wllama (llama.cpp compiled to WASM on CPU, npm 3.8.1 on 2026-10-02, works without WebGPU) can run a small model client-side on the static Vercel site. Keep the deterministic rule-based suggestion text as the default and treat the LLM wording as an opt-in enhancement.
projects.caveats: Not for Module B: Actions runners have no GPU, and wasm CPU inference is slower than native Ollama or llama.cpp. Models are hundreds of MB to a few GB for the user to download. WebGPU support varies by browser.

projects.name: cxcscmu/AutoGEO (ICLR 2026)
projects.module: A (rule and evidence source), B (evaluation design)
projects.what_to_adopt: Evidence and methodology, not runtime code. It mines 'content preference rules' from generative engines and scores a GEO score (visibility) against a GEU score (utility). Its datasets (HF cx-cmu/E-commerce, GEO-Bench, Researchy-GEO) can serve as extra simulator fixtures, and the rules can feed the evidence and source column of Module A's checks. Its explicit warning that rules are engine- and domain-specific supports showing evidence strength per check.
projects.caveats: Needs API keys (Gemini) and 2x A100 for the Mini model, so none of it runs in our stack. It rewrites documents, which conflicts with Module C's never-auto-rewrite principle; cite its rules only as suggestions. Check the dataset licenses before bundling (not checked).

projects.name: hellowalt/aeo-radar and anyin-ai/aperture (TS trackers, schema reference)
projects.what_to_adopt: Two small MIT trackers that show other shapes. aeo-radar (Next.js 16 + Prisma, prisma/schema.prisma) uses a pluggable 'subclass one base crawler per platform' pattern, which is close to our live-engine adapter interface. Aperture (FastAPI backend + TS UI) accepts any OpenAI-compatible base URL (Ollama/vLLM) and serves its provider list from `GET /api/providers`. Borrow the adapter-interface idea: `EngineAdapter { id, answer(query, opts) -> {text, citations[], consulted[]} }`, with `local-sim` as the first implementation.
projects.caveats: aeo-radar scrapes the ChatGPT web UI by default, and its own README warns about ToS and account bans, so don't copy that path. Both are small and not very active. Aperture's backend is Python.

projects.name: GetCito (ai-search-guru/getcito-worlds-first-open-source-aio-aeo-or-geo-tool)
projects.license: MIT (LICENSE.md says it is a derivative of Elmo), plus a CLA.md for contributions
projects.what_to_adopt: Nothing. It is an Elmo fork, so use Elmo upstream if you need anything from it.
projects.caveats: It requires a CLA and adds nothing over Elmo for a local-simulator design. The 'world's first open source' claim is false given the Elmo lineage.

sweep.gaps:
No open-source project, in TypeScript or otherwise, is an offline, frozen, local-model 'generative engine simulator' that tracks one page over time. Every tracker I opened (Elmo, GetCito, mcp-geo, aeo-radar, aperture, OpenCited, the AWS Bedrock sample) queries live engines with paid keys or scrapes consumer UIs. The GEO paper code and AutoGEO simulate an engine, but in Python, with API models, run once per experiment, with no scheduling or history. We have to build these parts ourselves:
(1) Corpus snapshotting. Fetch the creator page plus a fixed competitor and distractor set. Respect robots, extract with Defuddle, and store content_sha256 per page and a corpus_version, so the 'frozen control group' is actually frozen and a change is attributable to the creator's edit.
(2) The simulator loop. Chunk the pages, retrieve top-k (MiniSearch or Orama, optionally fused with transformers.js embeddings by RRF), then call a local model with the GEO-paper citation prompt. Pin model digest, seed, temperature 0 and prompt hash. Use structured output (Ollama `format` or node-llama-cpp JSON schema) so 1-4B models produce parseable [n] citations. Record retrieved-but-not-cited separately from cited (consulted vs cited).
(3) A TS port of the GEO impression metrics (word count, position, position-adjusted word count) and of Wilson intervals, which jianruntech/geo-score and footnoteone have only in Python, run over repeated samples or paraphrases. Report n and an interval on every number.
(4) A competitor feature diff ('winning pages have tables and schema, yours doesn't') that reuses Module A's check functions on the winning pages, so A and B stay in one engine.
(5) A GitHub Actions workflow that runs inside the free-runner limits. Verified: public repos get 4 vCPU / 16 GB / 14 GB SSD and private repos 2 vCPU / 8 GB. No GPU on standard runners. 6 h job cap. 10 GB cache per repo (enough to cache a 2-3 GB model). Cron times are UTC unless a timezone is set, minimum interval 5 min, runs 'can be delayed during periods of high loads' and queued jobs 'may be dropped', and scheduled workflows auto-disable after 60 days without repo activity. So '2 AM' must be configured as a UTC time or a timezone, and the job should commit a heartbeat so the cron stays enabled. Free minutes are unlimited on public repos and drawn from the account allotment on private ones.
(6) An EngineAdapter interface so the Perplexity, OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini adapters can plug in later and write the same record schema. Nothing we can depend on defines this for a local simulator.
(7) The trust UI: evidence strength and source per check, editable weights, accept/reject suggestions, and never auto-rewriting. None of the trackers do on-page, author-facing co-writing.
sweep.notes:
Method: I read each repo's README, LICENSE and schema files through the GitHub API (gh), checked npm metadata with `npm view` on 2026-10-23, and fetched the GitHub Docs, Node docs and ollama.com library pages. I also read the 2026-10-04 teardown (product_vs_elmo_result.json) first. Its design was Python (SQLAlchemy, RFC 9309 parser, bots.yaml, GitHub Actions committing JSONL), and the TS picks above map onto that plan one for one.

Model candidates for the control group. None of them have measured citation-accuracy numbers at 1-4B: I found no small-model citation benchmark, so run a quick bake-off on GEO-bench fixtures.
- qwen3:1.7b (1.4 GB, 40K context) and qwen3:4b (2.5 GB, 256K) on Ollama. Qwen3 is released under Apache-2.0, but the Ollama page doesn't state a license, so confirm on the HF card.
- granite4:micro / 3b (2.1 GB, 128K) on Ollama. Apache-2.0, confirmed on the HF card (released 2025-10-02). It lists RAG as a capability, but its model card shows no `documents` chat-template parameter and no RAG or citation benchmark scores.
- gemma4:e2b (4.6-7.5 GB). Used in the setup-ollama README example and in a 2026-09-16 article running it on Actions. Gemma terms are not an OSI license, so treat it as 'allowed to run, not to redistribute weights'.

Unverified and needing a smoke test: tokens/sec and wall time for one nightly batch on a 4-vCPU runner; whether Ollama `seed` + `temperature: 0` gives bit-identical outputs across runner hosts (CPU differences may break this, so store outputs and compare distributions, not exact strings); the GitHub artifact retention default (not on the limits page I fetched; committing JSONL avoids depending on it).

Avoid list: GPL/AGPL trackers from the prior teardown (AI2HU/gego GPL-3.0, usenotra/notra AGPL-3.0, promptclarity AGPL-3.0) are reference-only. GetCito has a CLA. wink-bm25 and lunr are stale.

Sources fetched: docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners, docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits, docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows, nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html, ollama.com/library/{granite4,qwen3,gemma4}, huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-micro, dev.classmethod.jp/articles/running-ollama-on-github-actions/.
